source: Authored by hand, NOT by author_flight.py. That tool authors an incoming flight from a passer position, and this drill has no incoming flight: the athlete starts with the ball.
startsWithTheBallNote: THE AUTHORING RULE FOR ANY DRILL THAT STARTS WITH THE BALL, followed here for the second time. Put BOTH keys where the ball actually is, in her hands, and name the smallest tidy arrival. DO NOT INVENT AN INCOMING FLIGHT TO SATISFY THE arrival FIELD. The two keys below say the ball is in her hands at 0.0 and still in her hands at 0.02, and both statements are true, so contact resolves to frame 0 and the ball is never in a flight state. An invented flight is visible: on netball_chest_pass, a first key out of reach with arrival at 0.20 put the athlete in a flight state for 16 frames of 96. Both failure modes are guarded mechanically in test_starts_with_the_ball.py.
arrivalNote: A formality, not a catch. arrival names the frame possession transfers, and for a pass that already happened before the drill began. 0.0 is refused by load_ball, which requires release < arrival, so 0.02 is the smallest tidy value.

keys.name: in_her_hands
keys.note: Where the ball is when the drill starts, at her chest. netball_two_hand_catch_chest's secured-ball numbers converted from torso lengths back to arm lengths.

keys.name: still_in_her_hands
keys.note: The same place. A flight of zero length is the honest description of a ball that never flew.

launchTargetNote: PROVISIONAL, and the same choice netball_chest_pass made for the same reason. 4.0 arm lengths is author_flight.DEFAULT_PASSER_AHEAD, the distance every feed in this library is thrown from, so the two passes and the six catches share one geometry. THE MANUAL DISAGREES and a coach must settle it: its passing drills stand players 5 to 7 m apart, which is 9.5 to 13.3 arm lengths, not 4.0 which is 2.11 m. up is 0.0 because a receiver of similar height has her hands at the height of this athlete's chest, where the stance frame is anchored.
launchSpeedNote: PROVISIONAL AND IT INHERITS AN OPEN QUESTION. 600 cm/s is author_flight.DEFAULT_SPEED_CM, the one speed the whole library uses, recorded in docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md as having no coach, no measurement and no source. A SECOND FACE OF THAT ENTRY WAS MEASURED WHILE WRITING THE LOB BRIEF and belongs with it rather than here: from a 135 cm chest release to a 145.4 cm catch the same 600 cm/s peaks at 225.4 cm over 5 m and 307.1 over 7 m; level at 135 it is 220.2 and 301.9. The pair of heights is named because without them the number is not reproducible, which cost this lane an exchange once already, so within the manual's own stated drill range the constant turns from a flat pass into a lob, with nothing in any file saying so. Authoring a different number here would invent a second unsourced constant, so this file uses the library's and names the question.
overheadReleaseNote: The launch is unchanged from the chest pass even though the release is 34 cm higher, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight. speedCmPerSecond is the HORIZONTAL component and the vertical is solved from gravity to reach the target, so a higher release produces a flatter arc to the same point without any change to this field. Refer to the Launch docstring in ball_track.py.
